question_text: If a = (b + c) cos θ, then prove that sin θ = (2√(bc)/(b+c)) cos(A/2).

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Square the given relation
steps.margin_note: No separate mark at this length. The target has a sine and the condition a cosine, so the bridge is sin² = 1 − cos². Square the condition first so it can be substituted.

recall.must_convey: That the condition is rearranged to cos θ = a/(b+c), squared, and sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ formed.
accept: rearrange to cos theta equals a over b plus c then square and use sin squared equals one minus cos squared
square the given relation and subtract from one
get sin squared theta as b plus c squared minus a squared over b plus c squared
cos theta ni square chesi one minus cos square teeskovali
form sin squared from the given cosine

steps.why: The answer is about sin θ but the condition gives cos θ. Squaring is the only route between them that stays exact.
common_mistakes: Taking the square root too early.
steps.memory_tip: The target is a sine and the condition a cosine, so the bridge is sin² = 1 − cos².

steps.label: Expand and use the cosine rule
steps.margin_note: No separate mark at this length. Expand (b+c)², then spot b² + c² − a² inside it — that is 2bc cos A by the cosine rule, and it is what brings the angle in.

recall.must_convey: That (b+c)² is expanded and b² + c² − a² recognised as 2bc cos A by the cosine rule.
accept: expand b plus c squared then b squared plus c squared minus a squared is two b c cos A by the cosine rule
use the cosine rule to bring the angle in
the bracket becomes two b c plus two b c cos A
cosine rule vaadi b square plus c square minus a square ni two bc cos A ga marchali
recognise the cosine rule inside the expansion
heard_as: b squared plus c squared minus a squared

steps.why: There is no angle anywhere until the cosine rule is used. Spotting b² + c² − a² is what turns a side identity into an angle one.
common_mistakes: Expanding but never grouping the b² + c² − a² together.
Writing the cosine rule upside down.
steps.memory_tip: Expand (b + c)², then spot b² + c² − a² inside — that is 2bc cos A and it brings the angle in.

steps.label: Introduce the half angle
steps.margin_note: One of the two marks — the method mark for the whole derivation. Factor 2bc out, then 1 + cos A = 2cos²(A/2) — which is where the half angle in the answer comes from.

recall.must_convey: That 2bc is factored out and 1 + cos A = 2cos²(A/2) applied, giving 4bc cos²(A/2)/(b+c)².
accept: take two b c out then one plus cos A is two cos squared half A so it becomes four b c cos squared half A over b plus c squared
use the half angle formula for one plus cos A
the four b c comes from two times two
one plus cos A ante two cos square A by two
factor and apply the half angle identity

steps.why: 1 + cos A = 2cos²(A/2) is the identity the whole family turns on. Its partner, 1 − cos A = 2sin²(A/2), is what answer 34.2 uses instead.
common_mistakes: Using 1 − cos A = 2sin²(A/2) here, which is the wrong half of the pair.
steps.memory_tip: A PLUS in front of cos A calls for the COSINE half-angle: 1 + cos A = 2cos²(A/2).

steps.label: Take the square root
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Everything under the root is a perfect square, so the root is exact — and sin θ is taken positive.

recall.must_convey: That taking the square root gives sin θ = (2√(bc)/(b+c)) cos(A/2).
accept: take the square root, four becomes two and the cos squared becomes cos half A
the root gives two root b c over b plus c times cos half A
square rooting gives the required form
root teeste two root bc by b plus c into cos A by two vasthundi
the answer is two root bc over b plus c cos half A

steps.why: √(4bc) is 2√(bc), not 4√(bc) — the 4 comes out as its own root. That is the one place the last line can go wrong.
steps.memory_tip: Everything under the root is a perfect square, so the root is exact and sin θ is taken positive.

insider_note: The PLUS version: squaring leaves 2bc(1 + cos A), and 1 + cos A = 2cos²(A/2). That sign inside the bracket is the only difference from the (b − c) sec θ question.
